newsitem.title: GERMANY: Fund managers cautiously welcome Telekom's debut.
newsitem.headline: Fund managers cautiously welcome Telekom's debut.

text.p: Portfolio managers gave a definite thumbs-up to the Deutsche Telekom share issue on Monday, but said that it was still important to wait and see how the share developed in coming months.

"The first and most obvious conclusion is that the Telekom issue has been very successful so far. How it performs from now on is important for long-term investors," said Murray Davey, head of European Equity Fund Management at Kleinwort Benson in London.
Davey said the premium of the share above its issue, which averaged around 15/20 percent during the day, was a balanced return.
In late electronic IBIS trade on Germany's DAX-30 blue-chip index, Telekom shares were quoted at 32.80 marks, off its day's high of 34.20 marks.
Deutsche Telekom's initial share price of 28.50 marks was announced on Sunday.
"A return of 15/20 percent is good, because it is not such a huge premium that the company feel aggrieved and it is around the level that people expected," said Davey.
"We have to look where we go from here. In the short-term we have to see the level of demand from the German institutions for Telekom shares," Davey said.
Fund managers said that one of the most important factors was whether or not people hold on to the stock rather than sell off quickly to make short-term gains.
A lot of interest so far has come from index funds, who track the DAX index and therefore have to invest in Telekom.
Sources in the fund management industry said the share could receive a four or five mark boost in the long run from the index trackers, especially if demand for the share outstrips supply.
"We will also have to monitor the degree of supply from investors who were only buying with a short-term view," said Davey.
Deutsche Telekom has insisted during the run-up to the sell-off that it is interested in long-term investors rather than short-term speculators.
German finance minister Theo Waigel reiterated this point at the launch of the Telekom IPO when he said: "We need a long-term equity culture here in Germany."

However, as the issue was oversubscribed over five times, fund managers said it was important that the buying interest from the large funds is matched by a selling interest from short-term investors if the stock was not to suffer.
